title: Lindernia antipoda: How to Spot and Control It in Rice Fields
metaTitle: Lindernia antipoda in Rice: Identification and Control
metaDescription: Lindernia antipoda, or lalagang, is a small broadleaf weed with lilac flowers in rainfed rice. Learn to spot it early and keep it from seeding.
excerpt: Lindernia antipoda is a small broadleaf weed that farmers know as lalagang. It has slender stems and toothed leaves, and when it blooms, the flowers are lilac. You will find it in rainfed lowland rice fields in the Philippines. This page shows you how to spot it between your rice hills and how it competes with your palay. Then it shows how to control it before it sets seed.

heroImage.alt: Sparrow false pimpernel (Lindernia antipoda), a broadleaf weed of Philippine rice fields

blocks.text:
Lindernia antipoda is a small herb from the figwort family, Scrophulariaceae. In English it is called sparrow false pimpernel. Farmers know it as lalagang. Its stems are thin, and the plant either spreads low or stands upright. Because it stays small, it can hide easily among young rice. Its pretty lilac flowers may look like a harmless wildflower, but in a palay field it is still a weed.

You will find it in rainfed lowland rice fields. This damo lives for only one season. Within one crop it sprouts, flowers, sets seed and dies. Seed is its only way to spread. Each small pod holds many tiny seeds that fall to the soil and wait there for the next planting. That is why a few plants left this season can bring many more next season.

Look low between the rice hills for a small plant with slender stems, either creeping or upright. The leaves are oblong to long and narrow, set in pairs, on very short stalks. Small teeth run along the leaf edges. Like other broadleaf weeds, the leaves are wide with netted veins, unlike grasses and sedges. Once the plant matures, small lilac flowers show up and make it easier to find.

items: A small plant with slender stems, spreading low or standing upright between rice hills.
Oblong to long narrow leaves on very short stalks, set in pairs.
Small teeth along the leaf edges, easy to see when you look closely.
Small lilac flowers that stand out against the green of young rice.

blocks.text:
Lalagang is small, but it competes with your palay all the same. Its roots draw water and nutrients from the soil your rice depends on, and it shares in the fertilizer you apply. Water can run short in a rainfed field, so every bit the weed takes hurts more. When many plants sprout at once, they crowd the gaps between young rice hills.

Because it is an annual that spreads by seed, every plant that flowers puts more seed into your soil. As a result, the patch comes back with the next crop, often thicker than before. Seeds can also mix with the harvested palay. Weedy spots give insects a place to hide close to your rice too.

items: Walk the paddy while the rice is young and look low between the hills. Pull lalagang plants before the lilac flowers turn to seed.
Hold rainwater in the paddy with strong bunds when you can. Tiny seeds of annual weeds come up more easily on bare, moist soil than under water.
Clean the bunds and field edges as well, so plants there cannot drop seed back into the bukid.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Broadleaves

If water and weeding cannot hold Lindernia antipoda down, choose an active ingredient that works on broadleaves at the age of your rice. The table follows PhilRice recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.
Keep Lindernia antipoda Out Next Season

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Prepare the land well: flood, plow, let the weed seeds sprout, then kill them when you harrow. Level the field so water covers it evenly.
Pull escapes before they flower and set seed, and carry them out of the paddy instead of leaving them on the bund.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [broadleaf weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.
Not Sure It Is Lindernia antipoda?

Take a clear photo of the leaf, the stem and the flower or seed head, then ask [Anee, the smart farm technician](/features/ai-agricultural-technician) in anee.io, in Tagalog or English. blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Lindernia antipoda

items.q: What is Lindernia antipoda called in the Philippines?
items.a: Farmers call it lalagang. In English it is sparrow false pimpernel, a long name for a small weed. It belongs to the figwort family. Since it has lilac flowers and stays low, it is easy to mistake for a harmless wildflower. In a rice field, though, treat it as a weed and pull it early.

items.q: How do I control lalagang in my rice field?
items.a: Begin with good land preparation and clean binhi. Keep water in the paddy when rain allows. Pull the plants by hand while young, before they flower. If many come up, choose a herbicide for broadleaf weeds that fits the age of your rice. Always follow the FPA registered label on the product.

items.q: Is lalagang harmful to my rice?
items.a: Yes, in its own quiet way. One plant does little, but many plants together take water, nutrients and fertilizer from your palay, most of all while the rice is young. Each plant that flowers also leaves seeds in your soil for the next crop. So pulling it early keeps the problem small and cheap.
